title: The One Where Underdog Gets Away

jokes.text: Rachel uses air quotes around 'job' when describing her waitressing position
jokes.setup: Rachel is earnestly explaining to her boss why she needs a $100 advance — she needs money for a ski trip to Vail because she's doing this 'whole independent thing'
jokes.punchline: She air-quotes 'job,' betraying that she doesn't really consider waitressing a real job — undermining the very independence she's claiming
jokes.explanation: A great character-specific joke that perfectly encapsulates Rachel's arc in Season 1 — she's technically trying to be independent but her attitude still betrays her spoiled origins. The air-quote is a small but devastating character reveal. High character integration because only Rachel, asking for an advance while explaining her independence, could land this.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Can I get an advance on my salary?

dialogue.speaker: Terry
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Terry tells Rachel: 'You're a terrible, terrible waitress. Really, really awful.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has just finished making her case for a salary advance, framing it with her independent-woman journey
jokes.punchline: Terry cuts through all her earnestness with blunt, doubled-down honesty — she's simply terrible at the job
jokes.explanation: The repetition ('terrible, terrible... really, really') is what elevates this from a generic insult. It's not just that she's bad — he has to say it twice, suggesting there's no polite way to soften it. Good economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, he's right. I am terrible at my job. I mean, I don't even know what a 'markup' is. I thought it was when you mark something up with a pen.

jokes.text: Immediately after being told she's a terrible waitress, Rachel brightly asks the room 'Does anybody need coffee?' and two customers instantly raise their hands
jokes.setup: Terry has just finished telling Rachel she's a terrible, terrible waitress
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately, obliviously demonstrates it by asking for coffee orders — and getting them — proving she can't even handle that simple task correctly (implied by Terry's amused 'Look at that')
jokes.explanation: The structural irony is sharp: she tries to prove herself competent immediately after being called incompetent, and Terry's dry 'Look at that' suggests she's already fumbling it. The joke works through juxtaposition and timing.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm doing so much better as a waitress now. I'm really getting the hang of it.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Excuse me, miss? Can I get some coffee?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, sure! Be right back.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Miss? Miss! I've been waiting for twenty minutes!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm so sorry. I completely forgot about you.

jokes.text: Terry watches Rachel finally take orders and says 'Heh. Look at that.' with resigned amusement
jokes.setup: Rachel has finally started doing her job after being told she's terrible
jokes.punchline: Terry's one-line reaction is darkly comic — this is apparently remarkable enough to note
jokes.explanation: A brief but effective button on the previous joke — the bar is so low that Terry finds it noteworthy when Rachel does the most basic part of her job. Works as a beat, doesn't overstay its welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Hi! Can I interest you in our specials today?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Also, I'm going to Vail next week and I'm a little short on cash, so if you could see your way to leaving a really generous tip, that would be amazing.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Sure.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Really?!

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Rachel asks a regular customer for an advance on her tips
jokes.setup: Having failed to get an advance from her boss, Rachel escalates to asking a customer — a complete stranger — for an advance on tips he hasn't left yet
jokes.punchline: The customer flatly says 'No,' and Rachel immediately pivots to apologizing for a prior spill, revealing she's been bad at the job all along
jokes.explanation: The escalating desperation is very Rachel. Asking a customer for a tip advance is a great absurdist premise that still feels character-grounded. The spill callback at the end adds a nice grace note — she's apologizing for yet another failure.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm not wearing makeup. I'm an actor/model.

jokes.text: 'Only 98.50 to go.' / 'I thought it was 98.50.' / 'Yeah, well it was, but I broke a cup.'
jokes.setup: Rachel sighs that she only has $98.50 left to earn for her ski trip ticket
jokes.punchline: When Monica points out it used to be $98.50, Rachel admits she broke a cup — meaning she's now in the hole even further, going backward on her goal
jokes.explanation: Tight, well-constructed little callback within the scene. The running gag of Rachel's dwindling finances works because it's specific (she broke a cup) rather than vague. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, so you're an actor slash model?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What about actor slash guy who wears makeup?

jokes.text: Ross and Monica argue about whether their parents are going to Puerto Rico — 'You're wrong.' / 'I am not wrong.' / 'You're wrong.' / 'I just talked to them.'
jokes.setup: Monica reveals their parents are going to Puerto Rico for Thanksgiving instead of the family tradition
jokes.punchline: Ross simply repeats 'You're wrong' like a child, which is funnier than any actual counter-argument — then goes to call Mom to verify, implying he knows he might be wrong
jokes.explanation: A mild but functional sibling dynamic joke. The repetition of 'You're wrong' without any actual argument is the joke — classic childish sibling behavior from two adults. Works but isn't particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What disease am I modeling for?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't know, they didn't say. But it's a big pharmaceutical company, so it's gotta be something serious.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh! Maybe it's something really bad! Like... like lupus or... or MS!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, why would you want to model for a serious disease?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Because it's a big pharmaceutical company! It's gotta pay good money!

jokes.text: Chandler: 'That's funny, I was thinking you look more like Joey Tribbiani, man/woman.'
jokes.setup: Joey announces he is now officially 'Joey Tribbiani, actor/model' while wearing visible makeup
jokes.punchline: Chandler reframes the title as 'man/woman' — a gender-bending jab at the makeup
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler wit — the parallel structure 'actor/model' → 'man/woman' is clean and quick. The joke is Chandler-specific in voice and delivery. Not exceptional but solidly crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I really hope I get this Lyme disease modeling job.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm gonna be honest with you, Joey. I really hope you do get Lyme disease.

jokes.text: Joey says he heard 'Lyme disease is open' for the free clinic poster campaign and says 'Good luck, man. I hope you get it.'
jokes.setup: The group is discussing which disease Joey will model for on the City Free Clinic posters — the asthma guy is considered cute
jokes.punchline: Joey casually mentions Lyme disease is available, and Chandler sincerely wishes him luck getting the disease assignment — treating a terrible illness like a coveted acting gig
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: the dark humor of hoping someone 'gets' Lyme disease, and the character-specific logic of Joey treating disease assignments like acting roles. The sincerity of 'Good luck, man' is what makes it land — no winking at the audience.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, will you make mashed potatoes with lumps like Mom's?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Lumps? Ross, I don't make lumps. Everything I make is smooth and creamy and perfectly textured.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: But Mom's had lumps. That's what made them special.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, Mom's were also a little dry and kind of sat there looking sad on the plate. I'm not doing that.

jokes.text: Chandler is 'boycotting all the Pilgrim holidays'
jokes.setup: Joey asks if Chandler is going home for Thanksgiving
jokes.punchline: Chandler says he's 'boycotting all the Pilgrim holidays' — a hilariously grandiose and vague political stance against Thanksgiving
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'Pilgrim holidays' is funny — it sounds like the kind of thing a child or a deeply unserious person would say. It plants the seed for the payoff of Chandler's parents' divorce story. Works as setup more than as a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: My grandmother's coming to the city, and my boyfriend's going to be there, and he's lunar.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'We're celebrating Thanksgiving in December because he's lunar.'
jokes.setup: Monica asks if Phoebe is spending Thanksgiving with her grandmother and her boyfriend
jokes.punchline: Phoebe explains they're celebrating in December because her grandmother's boyfriend is 'lunar' — Phoebe treats this as a perfectly normal explanation
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Phoebe — she doesn't even notice it's unusual. The word 'lunar' does a lot of work: it's just vague enough to be funny (is he a werewolf? does he follow the lunar calendar?) without needing explanation. Perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So what are you doing for Vail?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm totally going. Shoop, shoop, shoop.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: With what money?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Shoop, shoop, shoop.

jokes.text: Ross mimics Monica's 'Ooh ooh' excitement when suggesting inviting Carol, then cuts himself off: '...and will probably wanna bring her, ooh ooh, lesbian life partner.'
jokes.setup: Monica enthusiastically suggests ('Ooh ooh!') inviting Carol to Thanksgiving dinner
jokes.punchline: Ross mocks her enthusiasm by repeating her 'ooh ooh' sound while pointing out the awkwardness of inviting his ex-wife and her girlfriend
jokes.explanation: The mirroring of Monica's 'ooh ooh' is a deft structural move — Ross uses her own enthusiasm to underscore his discomfort. The phrase 'lesbian life partner' is funny in its formal specificity. Good character integration for both Ross's awkwardness and Monica's obliviousness.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Rachel, your debt went up by three thousand dollars. What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I may have... accidentally broken your coffee table.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: My coffee table costs three thousand dollars?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It was a really nice coffee table.

jokes.text: Ross: 'I just came by to pick up my skull.' Susan: 'What's it look like?' Ross: 'Kind of like a big face without skin.'
jokes.setup: Ross comes to Carol's apartment to pick up a skull he loaned her for a class — an unusual enough errand
jokes.punchline: Susan asks what it looks like, as if she doesn't know what a skull looks like, and Ross delivers the driest possible literal description
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy and structure. Susan's question is already a little absurd (who doesn't know what a skull looks like?), but Ross's answer — 'kind of like a big face without skin' — is a masterclass in deadpan literal description. It's technically accurate, totally useless as a description, and unexpectedly poetic. One of the episode's stronger jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why don't you invite Carol?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, uh, Carol will be bringing... her friend Susan.

jokes.text: Susan: 'Yes, heh, I'm familiar with the concept.'
jokes.setup: Ross has just described a skull as 'kind of like a big face without skin'
jokes.punchline: Susan confirms she knows what a skull is with arch understatement, essentially calling Ross an idiot without saying it
jokes.explanation: The follow-up to Ross's description. Susan's response is perfectly calibrated — she doesn't over-explain the joke, just lets the understatement land. 'Familiar with the concept' is a great comic phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I came to pick up my skull.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, not MY skull. It's a replica of a Homo habilis skull from the museum.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Wow, you guys sure have a lot of books about being a lesbian.'
jokes.setup: Ross is searching Carol and Susan's apartment for his skull
jokes.punchline: He notices and blurts out their extensive lesbian literature collection — awkward, oblivious, and quintessentially Ross
jokes.explanation: Functional awkward humor — Ross's social obliviousness is on display. The laugh comes from his total lack of filter, but the joke itself is fairly predictable.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A skull is like a skeleton head. It's bone. Round. With holes where the eyes go.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: Wow, Ross. Fascinating. I had no idea.

jokes.text: Susan: 'Well, you know, you have to take a course. Otherwise they don't let you do it.'
jokes.setup: Ross awkwardly comments on the many books about being a lesbian in their apartment
jokes.punchline: Susan deadpans that there's a certification course required — playing along with the absurd premise that being a lesbian is a regulated activity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Susan's deadpan response treats Ross's awkward observation as a straight question and answers it with absurdist bureaucratic logic. The split delivery across two lines ('You have to take a course. / Otherwise they don't let you do it.') is excellent structure. Highly quotable. Susan's dry wit is at its best here and it shuts Ross down perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So you two are reading lesbian books?

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: Well, we have to. It's a requirement. We had to get certified.

jokes.text: Ross picks up Yertle the Turtle and notes it's 'a classic,' clearly bemused to find it in the apartment
jokes.setup: Ross is snooping around the apartment, already uncomfortable
jokes.punchline: He spots a children's book and his instinct is to compliment it as 'a classic' — a dorky, nerdy reflex that breaks the tension
jokes.explanation: Mild character beat that sets up the next joke about reading to the baby. Works as connective tissue but isn't particularly funny on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: I read to the baby. Studies show that babies can hear in the womb.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I hate to break it to you, but I don't think the baby's going to remember Goodnight Moon. I mean, it's not like he's going to be born going, 'Hey, I know this one!'

jokes.text: Ross: 'The baby that hasn't been born yet? Uh, wouldn't that mean you're... crazy?'
jokes.setup: Susan reveals she reads Yertle the Turtle to the baby — the unborn baby
jokes.punchline: Ross's incredulity builds to calling Susan 'crazy' — delivered with his typical condescending academic skepticism
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'crazy?' and the building incredulity is well-structured. A functional joke that also characterizes Ross well, but the punchline itself is predictable.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Do you guys talk about me to the baby?

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: Oh, all the time. We call you 'The Geller.'

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Yeah, we're like, 'The Geller's on his way over.'

jokes.text: Susan: 'But, um, we just refer to you as Bobo the Sperm Guy.'
jokes.setup: Ross asks, with touching vulnerability, whether Susan talks about him to the baby
jokes.punchline: Susan confirms they do — but the baby knows Ross only as 'Bobo the Sperm Guy,' a nickname that is both hilarious and devastatingly reductive
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. It has everything: perfect setup (Ross's genuine emotional vulnerability makes the rug pull land harder), a punchline that is simultaneously funny AND character-revealing (Susan is withholding and dismissive of Ross), incredible economy, and remarkable originality. 'Bobo the Sperm Guy' is a uniquely specific, perfectly absurd nickname that reduces Ross's entire biological contribution to something comic and slightly degrading. This joke is comparable to the 8+ anchor examples — highly quotable, culturally remembered, and earns every point.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Babies can hear in the womb. We should test it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Put Ross's head in a turkey.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Look, if she's talking to it, I just think I should get some belly time too. I mean, not that I believe any of this.'
jokes.setup: Ross has been dismissive of talking to the unborn baby, calling Susan 'crazy'
jokes.punchline: He immediately reverses course and wants 'belly time' — but qualifies it by insisting he doesn't believe it works, saving face while completely contradicting himself
jokes.explanation: A lovely character contradiction — Ross the scientist dismisses it, but Ross the insecure father-to-be desperately wants in. The qualifier 'not that I believe any of this' is perfectly Ross. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'll butter your head!

jokes.text: Susan suggests Ross put his head inside a turkey to hear what the baby hears — 'This will seem a little weird. But you put your head inside this turkey...'
jokes.setup: Ross wants 'belly time' to talk to the baby; Susan offers to demonstrate how sound travels to the womb
jokes.punchline: The method involves putting one's head inside a raw turkey — presented by Susan completely seriously
jokes.explanation: The premise is delightfully absurd — using a turkey cavity as a sonic demonstration chamber. Susan's deadpan delivery of a completely ridiculous instruction is strong. The joke also functions as a visual setup for what's to come later in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I can't afford Vail.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'I'd very much like to butter your head.'
jokes.setup: Susan has suggested Ross put his head inside a turkey to understand how the baby hears sound in the womb; Chandler has declared he's 'totally behind this experiment'
jokes.punchline: Chandler's non-sequitur offer to butter Ross's head for the turkey-insertion experiment is gleefully absurd and sadistic
jokes.explanation: The formality of 'I would very much like to butter your head' is what makes this line. Chandler's gleeful enthusiasm for Ross's humiliation, expressed in polite terms, is classic Chandler. Short, punchy, and genuinely funny. The absurdism of the whole turkey-head scene is set up well.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, don't you notice anything different about the mail today?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Um, no? It's just mail.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Just mail? JUST mail? Look at it again!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, it's bills and catalogs. What am I supposed to be seeing?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: The POSTCARD! The one from Bermuda!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is this from Ben?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: NO! It's from me! I sent it! Three weeks ago! Do you know how long I've been waiting for you to notice?

jokes.text: Monica hands Rachel her mail and won't let her put it on the table — the bit where Monica holds out the envelope insistently
jokes.setup: Rachel is distracted and demoralized; Monica hands her mail and she says 'Thanks, put it on the table'
jokes.punchline: Monica refuses, holding the envelope out — forcing Rachel to actually take and open it, revealed to contain money from the group for her flight
jokes.explanation: A functional physical beat that serves the emotional plot more than pure comedy. The repeated exchange ('You can just put it on the table' / 'No. Here's your mail') gets a smile but isn't a big laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He made a 'traditional Thanksgiving feast' — which consisted of a frozen pizza and a bag of Doritos.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I mean, the turkey was a Hot Pocket.

jokes.text: Chandler's Thanksgiving dinner: tomato soup, grilled-cheese fixings, and a 'family-size bag of Funyuns'
jokes.setup: Monica has been laboring over a full Thanksgiving dinner; Chandler is handed a grocery bag
jokes.punchline: His 'traditional holiday feast' is tomato soup, grilled cheese, and Funyuns — a pathetic, childish meal that perfectly captures his Thanksgiving avoidance
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Funyuns' is the key detail — it's not just junk food, it's exactly the right kind of sad, specific junk food. 'Family-size' is a nice ironic touch for someone eating alone. Good character integration — only Chandler would have this as a holiday tradition.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I found out my parents were getting divorced on Thanksgiving. I was eating pumpkin pie.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It was a really good pie.

jokes.text: Chandler's Thanksgiving backstory: 'I have — and I remember this part vividly — a mouthful of pumpkin pie. And this is the moment my parents choose to tell me they're getting divorced.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is confused about why Chandler hates Thanksgiving; he agrees to explain
jokes.punchline: His parents timed a devastating life announcement for the exact moment he had a mouthful of pumpkin pie — the grotesque specificity of remembering that detail is both funny and deeply sad
jokes.explanation: A textbook example of dark comedy done right. The detail of 'mouthful of pumpkin pie' is simultaneously horrifying and funny — it's such a specific, minor sensory detail to anchor a traumatic memory. 'I remember this part vividly' signals that this is trauma-precise recall, not embellishment. Strong character integration: only Chandler would give this speech with this particular mix of humor and barely-suppressed pain.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, that's a real yam? I thought they only came in a can with the marshmallows on top!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, Rachel, yams are actual vegetables.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, what else have I been wrong about?

jokes.text: Chandler: 'It's very difficult to enjoy Thanksgiving dinner once you've seen it in reverse.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has explained that his parents announced their divorce while he had a mouthful of pumpkin pie
jokes.punchline: He implies he vomited — but describes it with clinical understatement as seeing the dinner 'in reverse'
jokes.explanation: The standout line of the episode alongside 'Bobo the Sperm Guy.' The phrase 'seen it in reverse' is a genuinely original, perfect euphemism for vomiting — it's factually accurate, visually evocative, and delivered with such casual understatement that it lands as a devastating punchline. The structure is flawless: setup (mouthful of pumpkin pie at the moment of parental bombshell) → delayed reaction → punchline delivered as an afterthought. This is genuinely exceptional comedy writing that meets the 8+ anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, I appreciate your input, I really do. But this is MY kitchen, and I would LOVE it if you would just... go find something else to do.

jokes.text: Joey meets his Macy's rival perfume spritzer and performs 'Aramis? Aramis? Aramis?' with full theatrical commitment
jokes.setup: Joey runs into the 'Obsession girl' from Macy's — a perfume model
jokes.punchline: When she says she was the Aramis guy, Joey performs an over-the-top recognition bit, making the mundane world of cologne spritzers into a glamorous industry
jokes.explanation: Joey's absolute sincerity in treating cologne spritzers like Hollywood legends is the engine of this scene. The triple repetition of 'Aramis?' mimics how fans react to celebrities. Works as character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey! I know you from the perfume counter at Bloomingdale's!

dialogue.speaker: Kristin
dialogue.line: Oh my God, yes! I remember you!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Watch this — *demonstrates exaggerated cologne spraying technique with elaborate arm movements* — you gotta spray it up in the air and walk through it. That's how the pros do it.

jokes.text: Perfume girl: 'What are you wearing?' Joey: 'Nothing.'
jokes.setup: The flirtation has been building; the girl asks 'What are you wearing?' — a natural perfume-industry question that doubles as flirtatious
jokes.punchline: Joey says 'Nothing' — meaning he's wearing no cologne/perfume, but the double meaning (he's wearing nothing) lands as an accidentally seductive answer
jokes.explanation: A tight, well-constructed double-meaning joke. The setup naturally generates both a literal and flirtatious interpretation of 'what are you wearing,' and 'Nothing' pays off both simultaneously. Maximum economy — one word is the entire punchline. Slightly undercut by being a fairly classic setup, but executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wow, that's amazing. You know, you really make this look like an art form.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I mean, the way you hold the bottle, the distance, the mist pattern... it's like you're Michelangelo painting the Sistine Chapel, except you're painting my neck with Obsession.

jokes.text: Joey's date makes an excuse to leave and says '...Um... Leave.' as her reason for needing to go
jokes.setup: Joey's date suddenly remembers something and says she has to go; Joey asks what she has to do
jokes.punchline: After a long pause, she can only say 'Um... Leave.' — her reason for leaving is simply leaving
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'Leave' is essential — it signals her complete inability to construct a lie. The tautology ('I need to leave because... I need to leave') is funny for its honesty. This sets up the reveal of why she fled: Joey's disease poster.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What perfume are you wearing?

dialogue.speaker: Kristin
dialogue.line: I'm not wearing any perfume, just my natural scent.

jokes.text: Joey gasps as he sees his own VD poster — reaction beat as he realizes why his date fled
jokes.setup: Joey's date has inexplicably fled; he hasn't figured out why
jokes.punchline: Joey spots a poster — presumably of himself as the VD model — and gasps, realizing why she ran: she recognized him as the venereal disease guy
jokes.explanation: A great visual payoff — inferred from context but clearly: Joey sees his own face on a VD clinic poster. The silence and gasp do the work; no dialogue needed. The structure is excellent: the mystery of why she left, plus 'I'd like to butter your head' plus the VD subplot all converge. Strong rewatch bonus because you know it's coming.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey guys, you won't believe what happened at my modeling shoot!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? Did they finally decide you could act?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, it was a VD poster. You know, for venereal disease awareness.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Joey!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know! And my family saw it. My mom called me crying, thinking I actually had a venereal disease!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, at least you're raising awareness?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's the thing! They didn't read the fine print. They just saw me on this poster looking all sick and miserable, and my whole family thinks I'm dying!

jokes.text: Friends: 'What? Saw what? No, we're just laughing. You know how laughter can be infectious.'
jokes.setup: Joey correctly guesses they all saw the VD poster
jokes.punchline: The friends' transparently bad attempt to cover — 'you know how laughter can be infectious' — is made funnier by the unintentional irony of 'infectious' in this context
jokes.explanation: The word 'infectious' is an accidental double meaning in this context (VD/infectious disease) that elevates what would be a simple deflection joke. Whether intentional or accidental by the writers, it's a genuinely funny piece of irony. Rewatch bonus for catching the word choice.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: My family thinks I have VD!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could you BE any more like a bad TV movie?

jokes.text: Joey: 'Set another place for Thanksgiving. My entire family thinks I have VD.'
jokes.setup: The group is already laughing about Joey's VD poster; he enters dejected
jokes.punchline: Joey's framing is perfect: not 'I'm embarrassed' but 'My family thinks I have VD' — delivered as a casual announcement, as if requesting a seat at the table is the natural response to family-wide VD belief
jokes.explanation: Excellent line. The economy is superb — two sentences that deliver the consequence, the punchline, and a deadpan request simultaneously. 'Set another place' as the logical response to 'my family thinks I have VD' is a perfect comedic non-sequitur. The line is immediately quotable and the delivery implied is beautifully resigned. One of the episode's top moments.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm not just cooking anymore, I'm flambeeing, sautéing, and... julienning! I'm basically verbing all the nouns in my kitchen!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yesterday I was so into it, I told Chandler I was going to 'dazzlingly dice' the vegetables. He just stared at me.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: But that's what great cooking is all about — the alliteration of ambition!

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Tonight, on a very special Blossom.'
jokes.setup: Joey has just delivered his devastating VD family news
jokes.punchline: Chandler's response is to frame the entire situation as a Very Special Episode of the show 'Blossom' — a meta-comment on the melodramatic sitcom conventions of the era
jokes.explanation: A sharp meta-sitcom joke — 'very special episode' was a real NBC label for issue-heavy episodes, and 'Blossom' was a peer show known for exactly this. Chandler's cultural savviness is perfectly expressed. The line is all delivery and timing; it works because it's completely unexpected as a response to Joey's announcement. Loses some points for being a dated pop-culture reference.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It doesn't feel like Mom's cooking without her yelling.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: ROSS!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Ah, now that's authentic.

jokes.text: Monica: 'Cider's mulling, turkey's turking, yams are yamming.' Then: 'What? I don't know.'
jokes.setup: Monica is checking on her Thanksgiving dinner preparations with characteristic intensity
jokes.punchline: She invents the verb 'turking' and 'yamming' by the logic of 'mulling,' then immediately acknowledges she has no idea what she just said
jokes.explanation: Monica's cooking-intensity generating nonsense verbs ('turking,' 'yamming') is character-specific and genuinely inventive wordplay. The immediate self-correction ('What? I don't know.') is pitch-perfect — she catches herself but can't stop. High character integration: only Monica, in full Thanksgiving command mode, would utter this and then look confused by her own words.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm so excited! My flight leaves in like three hours!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's great! Where are you going?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Aspen! I'm going skiing!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Skiing? Rachel, you've never skied in your life.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know, but how hard can it be? You just point yourself downhill and try not to die.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's... actually not terrible advice.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: See? I'll be fine! *makes skiing sound* Whooooosh!

jokes.text: Monica to Ross: 'Ugh. All right, that's it. Get out of my way and stop annoying me.' Ross: 'Well, that's closer. That's...'
jokes.setup: Monica says it doesn't feel the same without Mom in the kitchen
jokes.punchline: When Monica snaps at Ross — 'Get out of my way and stop annoying me' — he observes that THAT is closer to how Mom acts, rewarding her angry outburst as the most authentic Mom impression
jokes.explanation: A great sibling dynamic joke — Ross's observation that Monica snapping at him is the closest she's gotten to imitating their mother. The implicit joke about their mother is efficient and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm done!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Thank God—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm just getting warmed up!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: *throws food* And THAT is for eating my cheesecake!

jokes.text: Rachel: 'I got the ticket, I got the ticket. Five hours from now, shoop, shoop, shoop.' Monica: 'You must stop shooping.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has been doing her 'shoop shoop shoop' ski mime throughout the episode whenever she mentions Vail
jokes.punchline: Monica's exasperation — 'You must stop shooping' — finally gives voice to the audience's awareness that this has been happening all episode
jokes.explanation: A serviceable running gag payoff. 'You must stop shooping' is mildly funny but the joke has been done enough times that this feels more like a cap than a genuine escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, I have to say, your comedic timing with the food throws is really off. You're throwing too early in the setup.

jokes.text: Chandler mimes bombing the apartment with the pumpkin pie, complete with airplane sound effects
jokes.setup: Chandler is standing outside Monica's apartment with his sad Funyuns dinner, refusing to participate in merriment
jokes.punchline: He mimes a bombing run with the pumpkin pie — 'Look out. Incoming pumpkin pie.' with plane sound effects — a childish bit of physical comedy that contradicts his deadpan persona
jokes.explanation: A physical gag that works more on performance than writing. Moderately funny — Chandler doing childish physical comedy while refusing to enter is an okay contradiction, but it's not especially memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can't believe I have to spend Thanksgiving alone because of my disease.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, you made that up.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I know, but I'm committed to it now.

jokes.text: Chandler refuses to enter the apartment: 'No, thank you. I prefer to keep a safe distance from all this merriment.'
jokes.setup: Monica asks Chandler to just come in already
jokes.punchline: Chandler's formal phrasing ('I prefer to keep a safe distance from all this merriment') treats Thanksgiving cheer like a contagion — which given his backstory is darkly apt
jokes.explanation: 'Safe distance from all this merriment' is a perfectly Chandler turn of phrase — it makes joy sound like a hazardous material. Given the backstory we now know, it's also darkly poignant. The formal register ('I prefer') adds to the comic distance. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, so let me get this straight. You want them mashed, you want them fried, you want them baked, and you want them... what was it?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Julienned.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Julienned. Right. Does anyone want them boiled? No? Because I could boil them. I'm very good at boiling.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, it's not that hard.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Not that hard? Ross, I have five potatoes and five of you. One potato per person. How am I supposed to prepare the same potato five different ways?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You could cut it into pieces!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

jokes.text: Monica: 'We all laughed when you did it with the stuffing, but that's not funny anymore.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has been doing airplane bombing runs with the pumpkin pie
jokes.punchline: Monica's line reveals that the stuffing bombing already happened — the audience missed it, but Monica and the group already laughed once and are now done laughing
jokes.explanation: This line works because it implies an off-screen escalating bit — Chandler did the stuffing first and got laughs, so of course he escalated to the pumpkin pie. The 'not funny anymore' is funny precisely because it signals the group already found it funny once. Good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! Mom's not a threat, she's a promise.

jokes.text: Joey's mom makes Tater Tots as part of the Thanksgiving tradition: 'A little piece of turkey on your fork, a little cranberry sauce, and a Tot.'
jokes.setup: Monica has put together an elaborate Thanksgiving dinner; Joey asks where the Tater Tots are
jokes.punchline: Joey describes his family's Thanksgiving Tater Tot ritual with complete sincerity and specificity — it's ridiculous but he's entirely serious about it
jokes.explanation: The joke is Joey's total earnestness. Tater Tots at Thanksgiving dinner is objectively absurd, but he describes the turkey-cranberry-Tot combination as if describing a fine dining experience. Strong character integration — this is deeply, specifically Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, my mother used to say that peas and onions make everything better. Of course, she also said that a lot of things that weren't true, like that she'd always be there for me. But the peas and onions thing, I'm pretty sure that was real.

jokes.text: Joey: '...because of my disease.'
jokes.setup: Joey says it's bad enough he can't be with his family because of his disease — referring to the VD poster
jokes.punchline: The deadpan reference to 'my disease' treats the VD poster situation as if it's given him an actual venereal disease — or at least, the social consequences of one
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — two words ('my disease') do all the work, implicitly treating the poster stigma as equivalent to actually having the disease. The callback lands because of the strong setup in #31.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Oh my God! Did you see it? The giant balloon! It got away!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: They're looking for it everywhere! It's like... it's like a real-life version of that time I got stuck in the revolving door at Bloomingdale's!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But this is bigger! Much bigger! And it has a giant head!

jokes.text: Ross tells his unborn baby about choosing paleontology 'on a dare,' and concludes 'You have no idea what I'm saying, because, let's face it, you're a fetus.'
jokes.setup: Ross has been coerced into talking to Carol's belly; he starts telling the baby about his major
jokes.punchline: Ross suddenly acknowledges mid-anecdote that the baby literally cannot comprehend any of this — 'let's face it, you're a fetus' — combining self-awareness with the absurdity of the situation
jokes.explanation: Ross's scientific mind can't help breaking the fourth wall of the belly-talk. 'You're a fetus' is a great Ross line — technically accurate, delivered with gentle condescension to an unborn child. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's just the balloon.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Could be the actual dog.

jokes.text: The Underdog balloon escape: 'The most unbelievable thing has happened. Underdog has gotten away.' / 'No, no, the actual cartoon character.' / 'Of course the balloon.'
jokes.setup: Ross bursts in with major news about Underdog getting away
jokes.punchline: Rachel clarifies 'the balloon?' — Ross dramatically corrects 'No, the actual cartoon character' — then immediately reverses: 'Of course the balloon.' The absurd suggestion that the real Underdog escaped and then the self-correction is a quick two-step joke
jokes.explanation: A tight little misdirection bit — the false answer ('the actual cartoon character') delivered seriously and then immediately abandoned creates a quick double-take. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: How often do you see a giant balloon dog?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't know, Joey. How often do you see a giant balloon dog?

jokes.text: Phoebe whips the mashed potatoes while Ross is gone, ruining them. 'Ross needs lumps.' 'I thought we could have them whipped and then add some peas and onions. Why would we do that? Then they'd be just like my mom used to make it... before she died.'
jokes.setup: Monica turns around to find Phoebe has whipped the lumpy potatoes that Ross specifically requested
jokes.punchline: When Monica asks why, Phoebe explains her dead mother's potato recipe — turning a seemingly oblivious act into a sad personal backstory that Monica cannot argue with
jokes.explanation: A well-crafted character beat that escalates the potato chaos while adding Phoebe's specific brand of oblivious-but-sincere tragedy. '...before she died' is the turn that stops Monica cold and generates the laugh from discomfort. Phoebe's dead-mom card is deployed perfectly naturally here.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hi baby, it's your dad. I'm gonna talk to you about the miracle of life. You see, when a man and a woman love each other very much, they decide to... they get into a more *horizontal* position.

jokes.text: 'An 80-foot inflatable dog loose over the city? How often does that happen?' / 'Almost never.'
jokes.setup: Monica needs to stay and cook; Ross is trying to convince her to come watch the Underdog balloon
jokes.punchline: Ross frames this as a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity; Monica's dry 'almost never' grants the point without enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: 'Almost never' is the perfect response — technically accurate, completely deflating, and dryly funny. Ross's framing of the balloon as a rare opportunity is both true and absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey there, little guy. It's me, your dad. I just wanted to say... well, I wanted to be the first voice you heard. So, uh, hello. This is very special. Very intimate. Very... oh God, I'm talking to Rachel's stomach. I'm literally having a conversation with her uterus. Why is this happening? Why am I doing this? Okay, you know what? I'm just going to back away slowly and pretend this never happened.

jokes.text: 'That moment when we first saw the giant dog shadow fall over the park?' / 'But did they have to shoot him down? I mean, that was just mean.'
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel have just come back from the roof after watching the Underdog balloon saga
jokes.punchline: They describe it with the reverence of a film scene ('the giant dog shadow') and then express moral outrage at the balloon being 'shot down' — treating a deflated balloon as a tragedy
jokes.explanation: The sincere cinematic description of the 'giant dog shadow' is funny — it's described as if witnessing a natural wonder. 'They didn't have to shoot him down' treats the balloon with full animal personhood, which is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, where are the keys?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh... yeah, about that...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What do you mean 'about that'?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I don't actually have them.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: WHAT?!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I thought you said you had them!

jokes.text: 'Got the keys?' vs. 'Got the keys.' — the locked-out scene key misunderstanding
jokes.setup: As the group left for the roof to see the Underdog balloon, someone asked/confirmed about the keys
jokes.punchline: The group argues bitterly about whether 'Got the keys?' (a question) or 'Got the keys.' (a statement) was said — a distinction that is impossible to prove but completely changes who is responsible for them being locked out
jokes.explanation: A clever premise: the same words, delivered with a question mark or period, completely flip the assignment of responsibility. It captures a very real and relatable argument dynamic — the unprovable verbal dispute. Strong structure and a good escalation into the broader locked-out argument.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I have keys.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You have keys?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, I have keys.

jokes.text: 'Hey, hey. That tone won't make me go any faster.' / 'Joey.' / 'That one will.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is panicking about being locked out of the apartment with the oven on; Monica demands Joey hurry with the spare key
jokes.punchline: Joey pushes back on Monica's panic-tone, then immediately concedes when she adjusts — a perfect beat about the specific pitch at which Monica becomes persuasive
jokes.explanation: A precisely structured three-beat exchange that works perfectly. The escalating tone joke ('that tone won't... / that one will') is a great observation about Monica's specific terrifying register. Maximum economy — twelve words for a complete joke arc.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know, when I was your age, I had to make a big decision about my future. I thought long and hard about what I really wanted to do with my life.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Turns out, I became a paleontologist because Chandler bet me fifty bucks I couldn't do it.

jokes.text: Ross: 'You're just happy you don't have gills anymore.'
jokes.setup: Ross is talking to the fetus, having told it that it won't understand paleontology
jokes.punchline: He wraps up by telling the fetus it's 'just happy' about no longer having gills — treating fetal development stages as achievements to be celebrated
jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny and character-perfect: Ross the paleontologist/biologist defaults to evolutionary biology when trying to connect with his unborn child. 'Happy you don't have gills anymore' is a hilariously specific, scientifically literate thing to say to a fetus and is uniquely Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hello, little fetus. It's me, your dad. I'm here to talk to you about... dinosaurs. Did you know that the T-Rex had tiny arms? They were very small. Not useful for hugging. But I bet you'll have big arms. Strong arms for hugging your old man someday.

jokes.text: Ross refuses to sing to the belly, then immediately breaks into the Monkees theme song
jokes.setup: Susan suggests Ross sing to the baby; Ross flatly refuses — 'I am not singing to your stomach, okay?'
jokes.punchline: Within seconds, Ross is singing a modified Monkees theme with full commitment — the refusal evaporates instantly
jokes.explanation: Classic setup-reversal structure. The joke is the complete and rapid abandonment of Ross's stated position. Works well because we see the transition happen in real time.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey little guy, it's me, your dad. I'm gonna sing you a song.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Here we come, walking down the street. We get the funniest looks from everyone we meet.

jokes.text: 'Hey, hey, I'm your daddy / I'm the one without any breasts'
jokes.setup: Ross is improvising lyrics to the Monkees theme to sing to his unborn baby
jokes.punchline: His improvised lyric identifies himself to the baby by the most relevant anatomical distinction he can think of — the absence of breasts — as opposed to Carol and Susan
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed lyric joke. The logic is impeccable: in a household with two women, how does Ross distinguish himself to the baby? By the absence of breasts. It's anatomically correct, situationally appropriate, and genuinely surprising as an improvised lyric. The structure of the song parody landing on this specific detail is excellent. Comparable in quality to the 8+ anchor examples — it's original, economical, and the laughter it generates is earned through layered character context.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey baby, it's me, your dad. I'm gonna teach you so many things. I'm gonna teach you how to ride a bike, I'm gonna teach you how to throw a ball... I'm gonna teach you about girls, and... other stuff.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And I promise you, no matter what, I will always be there for you. Even if your mom and I... even if things don't work out between us, I will always be your dad.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And I'm gonna buy you the best toys, and we're gonna go to the park, and I'm gonna push you really high on the swings, and you're gonna laugh and laugh...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And when you're older, if you want to talk about anything, anything at all, I'll be there to listen. Because you're my kid, and I love you so much.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Can you go any faster with that?' / 'Hey, I got one keyhole and about a zillion keys. You do the math.'
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to unlock Monica's door with a large ring of spare keys
jokes.punchline: 'A zillion keys' and the suggestion to 'do the math' — Joey's math metaphor is itself mathematically absurd
jokes.explanation: Joey invoking mathematics while using 'a zillion' (not a real number) is a nice touch. The joke is functional but not particularly inventive. Gets a laugh from Joey's oblivious self-confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, and I'm not a lesbian!

jokes.text: Rachel to Monica: 'All right, smirky. If it wasn't for your stupid balloon, I would be on a plane, watching a woman do this right now.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is furious that the Underdog balloon excursion caused her to miss her flight
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'smirky' as a direct address to Monica is a mild cringe beat; then she demonstrates the ski motion she would be watching, stuck in the argument
jokes.explanation: Rachel physically demonstrating the ski motion she's missing in the middle of an argument is a good physical comedy beat inferred from context. The callback to the shoop-shoop gag makes it land better. 'Smirky' as an insult is mildly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh great, I'm stuck on a roof. That's just perfect. And here I thought my Thanksgiving was going to be boring.

jokes.text: 'No. I wouldn't say I had the keys unless I had the keys. And I obviously did not have the keys.' / 'Okay, all right, that's it. Enough with the keys. No one say 'keys.'' / 'Why would I have the keys?'
jokes.setup: The locked-out key argument has been going in circles
jokes.punchline: Monica declares 'Enough with the keys, no one say keys' — which someone immediately violates, and the word 'keys' gets repeated about a dozen more times
jokes.explanation: A classic escalation bit — declaring the topic closed while continuing to open it. The joke is in the futility of Monica's command and everyone's instant failure to comply.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm not flying tomorrow. I'm flying today. Today, Monica. In like, twenty minutes.

jokes.text: Monica/Ross 'Got the keys' argument continuation: 'I swear you said you had the keys.' 'No. I wouldn't say I had the keys unless I had the keys. And I obviously did not have the keys.'
jokes.setup: The locked-out crisis continues; the key argument is going in circles
jokes.punchline: Monica's logic ('I wouldn't say I had the keys unless I had the keys') is technically irrefutable and completely useless as a defense — the circular logic is the joke
jokes.explanation: Monica's increasingly emphatic self-justification is funny because her logic is correct but useless. The tautological structure ('I wouldn't say I had the keys unless I had the keys') mirrors the circular argument. Good escalation of the earlier scene.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm already going as fast as I can! You can't go faster than fast. That's not how speed works!

jokes.text: Monica's full Thanksgiving breakdown: everyone wants different potatoes so she's making multiple kinds; 'Does anybody care what kind of potatoes I want? No, no, no!'
jokes.setup: Monica has been accommodating everyone's potato preferences (lumps, peas and onions, Tots) while trying to cook an entire Thanksgiving dinner alone, locked out
jokes.punchline: She breaks down, revealing she never stated what she wanted and has been martyr-cooking for a group that never asked her preference
jokes.explanation: The breakdown is recognizably Monica — she creates her own martyrdom by refusing to state her needs while resenting that no one asks. The escalating potato list (lumps, peas and onions, Tots) has been building all episode for this payoff. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I can't believe I missed my flight! Do you know what this means? I'm never going to see those safety demonstrations again. Never! I've seen them dozens of times, and I always thought, 'When am I ever going to need to know where the emergency exit is?' Well, now I'll never know!

jokes.text: Monica sobs 'It's my first Thanksgiving!' in a comically high-pitched voice
jokes.setup: Monica's breakdown escalates; she's weeping about the ruined dinner
jokes.punchline: Her voice breaks into a cartoonishly high sob — 'It's my first Thanksgiving!' — undercut by Chandler: 'Okay, Monica, only dogs can hear you now'
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of Monica's voice going to dog-pitch is a solid visual-performance gag. Chandler's callback — 'only dogs can hear you' — is the better joke, landing as a precise, deadpan observation about the specific frequency of her breakdown.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, okay! Nobody say the K-word!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: The K-word?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yes! We've said it like fifty times and every time we say it, something bad happens!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Phoebe, that's not—

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Don't say it! I'm telling you, it's cursed!

jokes.text: Monica: '...and Mario gets his Tots.' [sobbing in high voice]
jokes.setup: Monica is having an emotional breakdown about her first Thanksgiving going wrong
jokes.punchline: She refers to Joey as 'Mario' — getting his name wrong in the heat of her breakdown — combined with sobbing in an unusually high register
jokes.explanation: Calling Joey 'Mario' during an emotional breakdown is a great detail — Monica's mind scrambles when she's overwhelmed. The 'sobbing in high voice' stage direction implies physical comedy from Courteney Cox that elevates the breakdown. The specificity of getting his name wrong while obsessing over Tots is pure Monica.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Keys! You know what I'm saying?

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Okay, Monica, only dogs can hear you now.'
jokes.setup: Monica's sobs have escalated to a comically high pitch
jokes.punchline: Chandler calmly notes that her frequency has exceeded human hearing range — delivering a scientific observation about her emotional state with total detachment
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The image of Monica's crying pitch exceeding human hearing is perfect — it's a precise, scientific way to describe emotional chaos. The economy is exceptional (nine words), and Chandler's detachment makes it land harder. Strong character integration — only Chandler would respond to a friend's breakdown this way, and it works because it comes from affection rather than cruelty. Meets the 8+ benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm doing everything! I'm cooking the turkey, I'm making the stuffing, I'm making the sweet potatoes, I'm making the cranberry sauce, I'm making the pies!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And nobody appreciates it! Nobody helps! You all just sit there and criticize everything I do!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: This is my first Thanksgiving as a host and I just want everything to be perfect!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Is that really too much to ask?!

jokes.text: Ross, still singing the Monkees theme, wanders in as the ruined dinner is discovered
jokes.setup: Everyone has just discovered the burnt Thanksgiving dinner after being locked out
jokes.punchline: Ross is humming/singing the Monkees song — completely unaware of the disaster — as the group surveys the carnage; tonal whiplash provides the comedy
jokes.explanation: A good callback that uses tonal contrast effectively. The joyful singing landing in the middle of burned-dinner devastation is well-timed. Ross's obliviousness is character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Is she okay?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Because like, this is the third time this week.

jokes.text: Ross, surveying the ruined potatoes: 'This doesn't smell like Mom's.' Monica: 'No, it doesn't, does it? But you wanted lumps, Ross? Well, here you go, buddy. You got one.'
jokes.setup: The Thanksgiving dinner is burnt and ruined; Ross makes the tactical error of commenting it doesn't smell like Mom's
jokes.punchline: Monica, at peak exasperation, snaps that yes — the burnt lump is the lump he wanted
jokes.explanation: A good callback payoff to the running potato-lumps bit. Monica's 'here you go, buddy. You got one.' is delivered with barely-contained rage, and the callback to the earlier lumps discussion makes it feel earned. Strong sibling dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: The dinner is burnt! THE DINNER IS BURNT! THEEEE DINNER IS BURNT!!!

jokes.text: Rachel: 'The plane is gone, so I guess I'm stuck here with you guys.' Monica: 'Hey, we all had better plans, okay? This was nobody's first choice.'
jokes.setup: The dinner is ruined and everyone is cranky
jokes.punchline: Monica's blunt declaration — 'This was nobody's first choice' — about the Thanksgiving they've all just made together is brutally honest and accidentally sweet
jokes.explanation: A functional joke that bridges the disaster and the inevitable heartwarming turn. 'Nobody's first choice' is an honest, slightly dark framing of their friendship that works.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Here are your potatoes, Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, these are... burnt.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes. Yes, they are.

jokes.text: Monica: 'So why was I busting my ass to make this delicious Thanksgiving dinner?!' / Joey: 'You call that delicious?'
jokes.setup: Monica defends her cooking effort during the shouting match
jokes.punchline: Joey's immediate, literal challenge — 'you call that delicious?' — with the burned turkey in clear view is blunt, stupid, and perfectly Joey
jokes.explanation: Joey's challenge during Monica's impassioned defense is a great character beat — he's not trying to hurt her, he just literally noticed the food is burned. The timing, right at Monica's most wounded moment, is perfect sitcom construction. Very Joey: food honestly ranks above social grace.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I can't believe I'm stuck with you people.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, where else are you gonna go? Your parents cut you off, your job pays nothing, and you live in my apartment.

jokes.text: 'Ugly Naked Guy... is having Thanksgiving dinner with Ugly Naked Gal.'
jokes.setup: The group discovers Ugly Naked Guy is not alone
jokes.punchline: The full reveal: Ugly Naked Guy has Ugly Naked Gal over for Thanksgiving — the naming convention alone is the joke
jokes.explanation: The joke is pure naming logic — if he's Ugly Naked Guy, of course she's Ugly Naked Gal. The parallel structure is funny because it's lazy and perfect at once.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know, in a way, this is beautiful. Fighting over dinner, arguing about nothing—this is what families do. This is tradition.

jokes.text: 'Ooh, ugly naked dancing.'
jokes.setup: The group has been watching Ugly Naked Guy and Ugly Naked Gal have Thanksgiving dinner
jokes.punchline: Someone announces they've broken into dancing — the escalating perversion of the Ugly Naked Guy experience
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfect escalation of the Ugly Naked Guy mythology. 'Ooh, ugly naked dancing' is compact and funny — the 'Ooh' does comic work suggesting both excitement and horror.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'It's nice that he has someone.'
jokes.setup: The group is watching the spectacle of Ugly Naked Guy and Ugly Naked Gal dancing
jokes.punchline: Phoebe cuts the comedic excitement with sincere sentiment — treating the Ugly Naked Guy situation as a touching romance
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's sincere empathy for the naked dancing man across the street is genuinely hilarious because it's completely earnest. The tonal whiplash — from group disgust/voyeurism to Phoebe's 'it's nice that he has someone' — is perfectly calibrated. This is a great character joke: only Phoebe would find the romantic angle. High character integration, excellent economy, and it lands with surprising warmth.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God! There's a woman in there with him!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A woman? Let me see!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Move over, move over!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Okay, who wants light cheese and who wants dark cheese?' Group: 'I don't even wanna know about the dark cheese.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is 'carving' — his grilled cheese sandwich for the Thanksgiving meal
jokes.punchline: He offers 'light cheese' vs. 'dark cheese' — the grilled cheese version of the traditional turkey carving; Joey's response about not wanting to know about dark cheese implies something disturbing has happened
jokes.explanation: A clever subversion of the turkey-carving tradition applied to grilled cheese. 'Dark cheese' echoes 'dark meat' perfectly. Joey's wary response about the dark cheese is the right instinct — funny because it implies a scorched, possibly alarming state of affairs.

jokes.text: Monica: 'I don't even wanna know about the dark cheese.'
jokes.setup: Chandler asks who wants 'dark cheese' from the grilled cheese
jokes.punchline: Monica's horrified refusal to contemplate dark cheese implies it's disgusting — adding a layer of food-snobbery to Chandler's makeshift holiday
jokes.explanation: Monica's reaction extends the grilled cheese bit nicely. Her refusal to engage with 'dark cheese' (Monica being a chef who finds the whole meal horrifying) is character-specific and economical. Good button.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know, it's actually really sweet. I mean, he finally has someone to share his life with. Someone who understands him.

jokes.text: Wishbone pull: 'You got the bigger half. What did you wish for?' / 'The bigger half.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Monica make a wish on the wishbone; Phoebe gets the bigger half
jokes.punchline: Her wish was the bigger half — a perfectly self-contained, tautological wish that needed no imagination
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly structured micro-joke. The setup primes for a sweet or funny wish; the punchline is that the wish was literally just the bigger half itself — she already had it, and that was the plan. It's a closed loop of perfect comic logic. Maximum economy (three words), original premise, and highly quotable. Meets the 8+ anchor benchmark.

jokes.text: Chandler's toast: 'I'm very thankful that all of your Thanksgivings sucked.'
jokes.setup: Chandler gives a genuine, heartfelt toast about how despite everyone's failed plans, being together is great
jokes.punchline: The toast pivots from genuine warmth to 'I'm very thankful that all of your Thanksgivings sucked' — Chandler can't resist the deflection even in a sincere moment
jokes.explanation: Chandler's toast is a perfect character moment — he builds toward genuine sentiment ('this has been really great, you know?') and then can't complete the sincerity without a dark punchline. 'I'm very thankful that all of your Thanksgivings sucked' is the episode's thesis and its best joke at the same time. The structure (genuine emotional buildup → abrupt pivot) is textbook Chandler. Highly quotable, deeply character-integrated, and genuinely funny. Meets the 8.0 anchor solidly.

dialogue.speaker: Ross

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What do you mean 'dark cheese'? There's no such thing as dark cheese.

jokes.text: Ross: 'Here's to a lousy Christmas.' Monica: 'And a crappy New Year.' All: 'Hear, hear.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has concluded his toast by saying he's thankful all their Thanksgivings sucked
jokes.punchline: The group extends the logic — if bad holidays bring them together, here's to the upcoming bad holidays too
jokes.explanation: A warm, funny capper that extends Chandler's toast logic to a group bit. 'A crappy New Year' as a sincere toast is a good inversion of holiday sentiments. Works as a closing joke because it's inclusive and group-driven.

tmdb_overview: Monica's first Thanksgiving dinner for the gang goes horribly wrong when they all run to the rooftop to see the runaway Underdog balloon from the parade.
insight: Thanksgiving episode delivers 75 jokes in 22 minutes, just missing elite status.
